title: The West Can't Top Parasite and They Should Stop Trying: A Saltburn Review

commenti.body:
Shameless clickbait title.

I haven't seen Saltburn yet but Emerald Fennel sucks, it's hardly fair to compare her to an actually brilliant director.

Have you actually read an Emily Brontë novel or are you just using that as shorthand for "English period fiction"?

I enjoyed Saltburn (mostly on a visual level), but Parasite is undeniably miles ahead.  I think part of the disconnect is that Emeral Fennel was born and raised ultra rich.  She is from the kind of family that Oliver infiltrates in Saltburn.  So it’s almost as if she’s writing from that point of view.  The lower class guy is unbelievably desperate to suck up to the upper class.  And when it’s revealed he’s a middle class guy, he becomes a psychotic, greedy schemer coveting wealth when he’s already fairly well off.

There’s no nuance.  And sure, the upper class family is pretty comedically flawed, but the film seems to make it a point of making the lower or middle class guy seem like a disgusting con man who just wants to kill the rich and take their place.

Parasite is about the cultural clashing of the classes, and the upper class’ eternal put down of the lower classes, and the lower class’ struggle to just live a better life.  The family in Parasite don’t even want to take the rich family’s place.  They just want to improve their impoverished life.  It’s got so much more to say, and treats everyone fairly.  Everyone in the film is a person with their own dreams and issues.  The class divides are where the subtle differences start to show.  The nuance and skillful commentary blows Saltburn out of the water.

You’ve missed a lot of what the film is doing. It’s not trying to be parasite. It’s not about class dynamics.

It’s about who has power and the way in which the world rewards style over substance. It’s more closer to American Psycho and Ingrid Goes West and a change in power dynamics between old money and the new. 

Oliver doesn’t represent the lower class or middle class. He represents someone who wants and is seeking power. 

[full breakdown](https://filmcolossus.com/saltburn-2023-explained)

I don't think Fennel really checked her privileges when making this one. The whole thing really just feels like an argument for the status quo, with the innocent rich staying on top of the villanous poor and middle class. Just shows to me how a private and film school education doesn't necessarily give the inspiration to say anything meaningful, especially when you can make something extraordinarily beautiful but meaningless

>Have you actually read an Emily Brontë novel 

*An* Emily Bronte novel? Isn't she famous for writing only one novel?

Well from Korean perspective Bong Joon-ho is from elite family as well. Just his mother could have hard life because her father well known author escaped to North with part of family during Korean war.

Ok, *the* Emily Brontë novel...

I don't see how the characters in Saltburn are anything like Emily Brontë characters besides being English and... some of them live in a big house? Seems like OP just chose a classic English novelist at random.
Haven't seen *Saltburn* but "the west" topped *Parasite* when it made *The Servant* in 1963. The title of this post is stupid.

Interesting. If that’s true, than I suppose it just says a lot about the two as filmmakers.  Bong obviously has more insight and empathy for the topics in question then Emerald.  To be fair though, Parasite was like Bong’s either movie and Saltburn is Emerald’s second.  So there’s still time to grow.  That being said, I think it’s likely that Bong will always be a more meaningful director.  Comparing their second films (Memories of Murder and Saltburn), the differences in depth are night and day.

I think overall Bong is pretty empathetic director taking into account how he treats his characters, reminds me a bit Coen brothers in this aspect. 

There is also pretty big difference between being elite from fast developing country and being elite from one of the richest countries in the world for ages. Because elite from poorer county while traveling or studying abroad to western countries can have kind experience of being poor. And if his countries develop meaning of being rich or elite change with rising improvement of the living standard.

That’s very true.  Elite means different things in different economic climates or developing countries.  You could be elite in one country, but middle class or even lower in a different one.

And I agree whole heartedly with what you say about Bong being a very empathetic director.

Triangle of Sadness is a solid tie with Parasite, five stars each. The Menu, while maybe not in the same ballpark, is excellent. Glass Onion was a lot of fun. I haven't seen Saltburn yet, but if these other three are examples of what filmmakers should stop trying to do I couldn't disagree more.

That's all fine and dandy, but setting up the movie the way they did and not expecting people to look at it from the perspective of class is wild

When you watch something like Parasite, you see the way class dynamics get emphasized scene by scene through dialogue and mise en scene and little subplot like the dad’s smell while driving. Even the opening shot where you look out the street-level window then the camera lowers to find the main characters. That movement downward is a point of emphasis.

Saltburn doesn’t have those same class-focused points of emphasis. The few it does feature end up being red herrings that pretty much imply that the class-view was incorrect. All the major emphases towards ideas of fitting in, power dynamics, and style vs substance.

So I think they were hoping people would follow that train of thought.

But the initial framing grounds people so deeply in the class thing that it becomes easy to go with the initial read rather than adjusting like the film wants you to. 

It’s similar to how when Fight Club came out all these people kept judging it through the lens of a superficial fighting movie because that’s what the name and trailer emphasized.

Here for the servant mention. I bought that on Criterion not long ago. It's so good. Parasite is basically a modern hybrid of The Servant and Kurosawa's High+Low.  That's not a slight against it, but I do have to admit the two that inspired it are even better.

>But the initial framing grounds people so deeply in the class thing that it becomes easy to go with the initial read rather than adjusting like the film wants you to.

I'm not disputing your take on the themes of the film.  I'm just saying structuring the movie the way they did, it's insane for them to think that the takeaway for a lot of people who watch is going to involve class to some degree. It's by far the loudest and most consistent theme on the screen. Of course that's going to be a huge general takeaway regardless of the intentions. 

You could tell the story of power dynamics anywhere. The context of the characters and setting are going to play a large role in peoples takeaway
I agree with all of that!
This. In Britain it's far too touchy a subject to skirt around that not attempting to reflect on it just comes across as a bit ignorant.

Well ... if a filmmaker can get their own spin on something and get something great and creative out of it, it's great. However, you can still make a movie in that ballpark and have it suck. Let me know what you think after you watched it!

For my part I have a policy of not attributing to artist worldview what may just come down to flaws in writing. I have read so many spec screenplays that were written by ardent, good-natured feminists that had events or themes that actually came off as misogynistic, that I think its very easy to make art that is inadvertent with its message. I agree BJH is another tier of director from EF, so far, and I didn’t care for Saltburn (and love almost all of BJH’s work so far), but am just making the point it behooves us to be careful in attributing characters traits like empathy or whathaveyou to the artist vs the artwork.
